{{short description|Short-term changes in the Earth's magnetic field}}
'''Geomagnetic secular variation''' is the changes in the [[Earth's magnetic field]] on time scales of about a year or more. These changes mostly reflect changes in the [[Internal structure of Earth|Earth's interior]], while more rapid changes mostly originate in the [[ionosphere]] or [[magnetosphere]].<ref name=MerrillCh2>{{harvnb|Merrill|McElhinny|McFadden|1996|loc=Ch. 2}}</ref>

The geomagnetic field changes on time scales from milliseconds to millions of years.  Shorter time scales mostly arise from currents in the [[ionosphere]] and [[magnetosphere]], and some changes can be traced to [[geomagnetic storms]] or daily variations in currents.  Changes over time scales of a year or more mostly reflect changes in the Earth's interior, particularly the iron-rich [[Outer core|core]].  These changes are referred to as ''[[secular variation]]''.<ref name=MerrillCh2/> In most [[Scientific modelling|models]], the secular variation is the amortized time [[derivative]] of the magnetic field <math>\mathbf{B}</math>, <math>\dot{\mathbf{B}}</math>. The second derivative, <math>\ddot{\mathbf{B}}</math> is the ''secular acceleration''.<ref name=Fournier>{{cite journal |last1=Fournier |first1=Alexandre |last2=Aubert |first2=Julien |last3=Lesur |first3=Vincent |last4=Thébault |first4=Erwan |title=Physics-based secular variation candidate models for the IGRF |journal=Earth, Planets and Space |date=December 2021 |volume=73 |issue=1 |pages=190 |doi=10.1186/s40623-021-01507-z|doi-access=free |bibcode=2021EP&S...73..190F }}</ref>

==Recent changes==
[[Image:Earth Magnetic Field Declination from 1590 to 1990.gif|thumb|right|300px|Estimated declination contours by year, 1590 to 1990 (click to see variation).]]
[[Image:Geomagnetic_axial_dipole_strength.svg|thumb|right|300px|Strength of the axial dipole component of Earth's magnetic field from 1600 to 2020, according to three models.]]
Secular variation can be observed in measurements at magnetic observatories, some of which have been operating for hundreds of years (the [[Kew Observatory]], for example).  Over such a time scale, [[magnetic declination]] is observed to vary over tens of degrees.<ref name=MerrillCh2/> A movie on the right shows how global declinations have changed over the last few centuries.<ref name=declination>{{harvnb|Jackson|Jonkers|Walker|2000}}</ref>

To analyze global patterns of change in the geomagnetic field, geophysicists fit the field data to a [[Spherical harmonics|spherical harmonic]] expansion (see [[International Geomagnetic Reference Field]]). The terms in this expansion can be divided into a [[Dipole|dipolar]] part, like the field around a bar magnet, and a non-dipolar part. The dipolar part dominates the geomagnetic field and determines the direction of the [[Geomagnetic pole#North Geomagnetic Pole|geomagnetic poles]]. The direction and intensity of the dipole change over time.<ref name=MerrillCh2/> Over the last two centuries the dipole strength has been decreasing at a rate of about 6.3% per century. At this rate of decrease, the field would reach zero in about 1600 years.<ref name=GSC>{{harvnb|CGS|2011}}</ref> However, this strength is about average for the last 7 thousand years, and the current rate of change is not unusual.<ref name=Constable_dipole>{{harvnb|Constable|2007}}</ref>

A prominent feature in the non-dipolar part of the secular variation is a ''westward drift'' at a rate of about 0.2 degrees per year.<ref name=GSC/> This drift is not the same everywhere and has varied over time. The globally averaged drift has been westward since about 1400 AD but eastward between about 1000 AD and 1400 AD.<ref name=Dumberry>{{harvnb|Dumberry|Finlay|2007}}</ref>

==Paleomagnetic secular variation==
Changes that predate magnetic observatories are recorded in archaeological and geological materials. Such changes are referred to as ''paleomagnetic secular variation'' or ''paleosecular variation (PSV)''. The records typically include long periods of small change with occasional large changes reflecting [[geomagnetic excursion]]s and [[geomagnetic reversal]]s.<ref name=TauxeCh1>{{harvnb|Tauxe|1998|loc=Ch. 1}}</ref>

The Levantine Iron Age anomaly was a fast and spatially localized geomagnetic positive anomaly which took place in the [[Levant]], with maxima at about 950, 750 and 500 BCE.<ref name="Rivera-2023">{{cite journal |last1=Rivera |first1=Pablo |last2=Pavón-Carrasco |first2=F. Javier |last3=Osete |first3=María Luisa |title=Modeling geomagnetic spikes: the Levantine Iron Age anomaly |journal=Earth, Planets and Space |date=2023 |volume=75 |issue=133 |doi=10.1186/s40623-023-01880-x |doi-access=free |bibcode=2023EP&S...75..133R |hdl=10261/358784 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>
